definition.text: Work to improve the environmental health of a river or stream, for biodiversity, recreation, flood management or landscape.

facts.text: Approaches split into form-based restoration, which physically alters the stream, and process-based restoration, which restores natural water and sediment processes.
It differs from river engineering, which alters water bodies for navigation, flood control or water supply without an ecological aim.
Activities range from fixing a culvert or removing a weir that blocks fish, to stabilizing banks, restoring riparian zones or adding constructed wetlands.
Projects usually begin by assessing climate, geology, hydrology, sediment transport, channel shape and flood records.
A US database built in the 2000s held over 35,000 stream restoration projects.
Its effectiveness remains poorly measured because of thin data, too little monitoring and differing yardsticks.
It is entering law, for example through the European water framework's commitment to restore surface waters.

title: Form-based stream restoration

definition.text: Restoration that changes a stream channel's physical shape to improve its condition.

facts.text: Tools include deflectors, cross-vanes, weirs and step-pools, engineered log jams, bank stabilization and channel reconfiguration.
It gives immediate change but can fail when degradation comes from a wider area.
Critics say it works at too small a scale and aims for what people think a stream should look like, not its geomorphic setting.

contested_note: Scientists criticize form-based restoration as working at too small a scale and imposing a socially preferred stream shape.

definition.text: Restoration that rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form.

facts.text: It has grown in popularity since the mid-1990s as a more ecosystem-centred approach.
It restores connections between stream and floodplain and along the stream, often by removing levees, dams or grade controls.
It aims to make the system as resilient as possible and need little maintenance, though benefits can take time to appear.

title: Natural Channel Design

definition.text: A US method from the 1990s that classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed and then redesigns the channel to a target form.

facts.text: Its design phase has 8 phases and 40 steps.
Fluvial geomorphologists call it a 'cookbook' approach that untrained practitioners misuse, leading to failures.
Its focus on channel stability can limit a stream's ability to adapt.

contested_note: Fluvial geomorphologists criticize the method as a cookbook approach that can cause project failures.

title: Stream corridor (freedom space)
article: Stream restoration#Implementing a minimum stream corridor width

definition.text: A band of land, set by a stream's hydrology and geomorphology, within which the stream is left free to move with minimal intervention.

facts.text: The idea goes by many names: river corridor in the US, room for the river in the Netherlands, freedom space in France, making space for water in the UK.
A cost-benefit analysis found it could pay off long term through lower maintenance costs, less erosion and flood damage, and ecological services.

definition.text: Placing large wood in a stream to recreate the natural log jams that channelization and beaver removal took away.

facts.text: Log jams add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow.

definition.text: Stabilizing stream banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap and gabions.

facts.text: Roots from sprouting live branches anchor the soil and prevent erosion.
This makes bioengineered structures more natural and adaptable than hard engineering.
Some bank erosion is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riparian habitats.

definition.text: A dam built by beavers, creating a pond that protects them from predators and stores food for winter.

facts.text: By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a keystone species and ecosystem engineers.
In their native range, beaver dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks.
The dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and sustaining flow in dry spells.
Bacteria in the debris behind dams turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some pesticides.
Beaver ponds trapped 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams in an Alberta study.
Dams typically run from a few metres to about 100 metres long; the largest known is 775 metres.
They can flood farmland, roads and railways, and introduced beavers in Tierra del Fuego are considered a plague.
Abandoned dams leave wetlands that become meadows and then forest, slowly building up valley bottomland.

definition.text: A human-built structure that imitates a beaver dam, to gain its benefits or to attract beavers to settle.

facts.text: Builders may drive wooden posts into the stream bed to hold branches that would otherwise wash away.
Even if beavers never take over, analogs provide many of the benefits of natural dams, such as water retention and wetland ponds.
